title: O my eyes
hookLine: the eyes are told the Lord put His light in them, so see Him in all (Anand, the eyes)

lines: THE WORLD THE SAME, THE SIGHT NEW.
cards: There's a kind of video people love to share: a child getting her first pair of glasses. She puts them on in the optician's chair, looks up at her mother, and her face changes. Then she looks out the window and points.
Leaves. She hadn't known trees had separate leaves. Nothing outside had changed.
Her sight had. The Anand has a pauri like that moment, spoken straight to the eyes.

teach.h: AE NAETRAHU MAIRIHO: O MY EYES.
teach.b: After the body, Guru Amar Das speaks to the eyes: ae naetrahu mairiho, O my eyes. In paraphrase: the Lord has put His light in you, so look on no one but the Lord. That could sound like a command to stop seeing the world.

teach.h: THIS WORLD YOU SEE IS THE LORD'S FORM.
teach.b: Read on, and it means nearly the opposite: this whole world you see is the Lord's own form; the Lord's form is what comes into view. So the eyes aren't told to look away from people and places.
They're told what they're actually looking at. Then the turn, and it's honest. By the Guru's grace, Guru Amar Das says, I understood: wherever I look, the Lord is one, and there's no other.

teach.h: THESE EYES WERE BLIND, NOW DIVINE SIGHT.
teach.b: And the closing line: these eyes were blind, and meeting the True Guru, they received divine sight. The phrase is dib drisat, sight that sees more than surfaces. Like the child in the glasses, the world hasn't changed.
The eyes have. Yesterday the light was placed in the body.
Today the same light is in the eyes, and with it they're meant to find the same light in everything they see: light looking at light.
Sikh teachers draw from this a reason the way you look at someone matters: the stranger on the bus, the person serving you, the one you find hard.
The pauri doesn't ask the eyes to close. It asks them to see Him.

how: This pauri is part of the full Anand Sahib that many Sikhs recite each morning; seeing the one light in everyone is often given as the ground of Sikh equality, lived out in sangat and langar.

o: a lamp lit to read the Granth
a tear shed in deep prayer

games.q: the eyes pauri — tap the pairs.

s: the eyes pauri tells the eyes to stop looking at the world
it says the world they see is the Lord's form; it changes what they see, not where they look.
the pauri admits the eyes were blind
and says that meeting the True Guru they received divine sight.
the light in the eyes is a different light from the one in the body
the same light the Anand says was placed in the body.

games.q: the Anand tells the eyes to look on no one but the Lord. what does it say they should do with the world?
o: see it as the Lord's own form.
games.why: the next lines say the whole world the eyes see is the Lord's form: the eyes don't look away, they see what's there.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll see today, someone ordinary or someone difficult, and picture their face clearly: the way they stand, the look they get when they're tired.
Hold the Anand's line beside the picture, the same light placed in you was placed in them, and breathe, without forcing a feeling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, with that face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Naetr, eye. Ae naetrahu mairiho: the Anand tells the eyes the Lord's light is in them, that the world they see is His form, and that meeting the True Guru gives divine sight.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: naetr, eye; the Anand addresses the eyes as naetrahu, O eyes.

carryVoice: Your line: eyes, see him. The same world, seen with new sight. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ramkali M3, Anand, the eyes pauri (ae naetrahu mairiho), Ang 922
